memory_leads.lead: Vessel technical management separates economic ownership and commercial employment from the continuous engineering-control layer. Technical managers and superintendents can prioritize maintenance, defects, spares, service attendance and drydock scope while onboard engineering teams observe and execute day-to-day work.

A planned-maintenance system is structurally a queue of due obligations rather than proof of physical condition. A task can be not-yet-due, due, overdue, deferred, in progress or closed, and those states should remain distinct from whether the underlying equipment is actually degraded or failed.

Defect management forms a parallel open-item backlog. Discovery, initial severity assessment, temporary mitigation, shore escalation, parts/service planning, repair and closure can occur on different clocks, so an open defect should not be collapsed into either immediate off-hire or harmlessness.

Critical-equipment status adds consequence weighting to the backlog. The same number of open items can imply very different operational risk depending on whether they affect redundancy, propulsion, steering, power, cargo-handling, navigation, safety or pollution-prevention functions.

Condition monitoring creates an observation stream distinct from scheduled maintenance and breakdowns: trends in vibration, temperatures, pressures, oil condition, wear or performance can trigger inspection or intervention before outright failure, but exact readings and thresholds are vessel- and maker-specific.

Spares management is an inventory state machine: onboard stock, minimum/critical stock expectation, requisition, approval, order, manufacture or sourcing, shipment, customs/agent handoff, receipt onboard and consumption. A repair may be technically understood yet blocked by one missing component.

Procurement and expediting create a shore-side dependency layer between engineering need and physical part availability. Purchase approval, supplier confirmation, lead-time revision, logistics routing and vessel-port matching can materially change repair timing without changing the defect itself.

Maker or specialist service attendance is another schedulable resource. A vessel, spare part and technician may need to coincide at a suitable port or yard, so service windows and travel/logistics can govern closure even when equipment and labor capability exist separately.

Technical managers repeatedly choose among repair afloat, temporary mitigation, controlled deferral, port-call intervention and bundling into a future drydock. The choice depends on safety/approval boundaries, operational consequence, parts and specialist availability, trading schedule, cost and expected remaining asset life.

Maintenance budgets are allocation controls rather than physical-state measurements. Budget approval, variance, postponement or reprioritization can change when work occurs, while mandatory safety or class-related items may have much less economic discretion than cosmetic or convenience work.

Redundancy and temporary operating arrangements can preserve commercial availability after a defect while increasing exposure to a second failure or narrowing operating limits. Point-in-time replay therefore needs degraded-but-operable states rather than a simple available/unavailable vessel bit.

Maintenance closure itself has layers: work physically performed, onboard function checked, superintendent or owner acceptance, class/flag or maker evidence where applicable, defect-list closure and later reliability confirmation need not be simultaneous.

Repeated failures and fleet-wide defect patterns can turn one-vessel maintenance into organizational learning: sister-vessel checks, revised spares policy, changed maintenance frequency, modification campaigns or drydock bundling can emerge without proving a universal root cause.

P056 drydock memory is refined because yard specifications are partly the accumulated output of prior due items, defects, condition trends, regulatory work and deferred modifications rather than a clean project invented at docking time.

Atlas effective-capacity memory is refined because technical readiness can absorb capacity through planned maintenance, degraded operation, waiting for spares/service, unplanned off-hire and delayed return even when the fleet count and nominal deadweight/TEU are unchanged.

P053 survey/inspection memory is refined because observations can enter defect or maintenance queues, while later opening-up, repair and testing create new observations that should append to rather than overwrite the original condition record.

P055 end-of-life memory is refined because a growing defect backlog, parts obsolescence, repeated failures and future maintenance/drydock burden can alter the life-extension-versus-recycling decision even before a single catastrophic repair estimate exists.

The atlas already treats maintenance, retrofit and operational availability as effective-supply factors; P057 adds the continuous backlog, procurement and closure state machine rather than rediscovering that broad relationship.

P056 already introduced technical managers, service engineers and spares as project dependencies. P057 reuses those actors in continuous vessel management and does not create a second semantic owner for repair-project execution.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Maintenance programs, defect status and criticality are vessel-, manager-, class-, flag- and rule-vintage-specific source facts.
Measurements, diagnostic thresholds and causal findings require technical records and authoritative Evidence.
Inventory, procurement, commercial and service-execution facts are company- and vessel-specific.
Provider identity, current capability and rankings are source-first factual questions outside blind Memory.

stop_reason: The continuous technical-management lifecycle is populated from maintenance due states and defect backlog through criticality, condition monitoring, spares/procurement, service attendance, repair-versus-defer decisions, budget allocation, degraded operation, closure and fleet-level reliability learning. Further recall becomes interval-, defect-, equipment-, quantity-, purchase-order-, budget-, measurement-, failure-, provider- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation and not technical, maintenance, class, regulatory, safety, procurement or investment advice; no maintenance interval, defect, critical-equipment status, condition reading, spares quantity, purchase order, budget, failure diagnosis, service record, provider capability or vessel condition is verified.
